title: Canada Deports 3,323 Indians in Six Months as 2026 Heads for Record High
excerpt: India has overtaken Mexico as the top nationality for enforced removals from Canada, with nearly 7,000 more Indian nationals in the deportation pipeline.
body:
• Canada removed 3,323 Indian nationals in the first half of 2026, putting the year on track to nearly double 2025's total of 3,779 deportations
  • India overtook Mexico as the most deported nationality for the first time since 2020, accounting for 32.5% of all removals in Q1 2026
  • Nearly 7,000 Indian nationals remain in the Canada Border Services Agency's "removal in progress" inventory, the largest group on record

Canada deported 3,323 Indian nationals in the first six months of 2026, according to data from the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), placing the country on pace to nearly double last year's total and setting what would be a record high for Indian deportations from Canada.

The figures mark a dramatic escalation in enforcement. In all of 2025, Canada removed 3,779 Indian nationals. The first-half 2026 numbers have already reached 88% of that full-year figure with six months remaining.

India Overtakes Mexico as Top Deportee Group

The data represents a structural shift in Canada's deportation landscape. In Q1 2026 alone, the CBSA removed 1,712 Indian citizens — 32.5% of the 5,260 total removals carried out in the quarter. This pushed India ahead of Mexico, which recorded 743 removals in the same period, marking the first time since 2020 that Indians accounted for the highest number of deportations.

In 2025, Mexican nationals led annual removals with 4,837 compared to India's 3,779. The reversal in 2026 has been swift and decisive.

"This trend reflects a combination of higher claim volumes, processing outcomes, and stricter enforcement — not necessarily higher non-compliance rates."

— NNC Immigration Brief

A Pipeline That Keeps Growing

Beyond the completed removals, the pending caseload points to continued momentum. As of mid-April, 6,980 Indian nationals sat in the CBSA's "removals in progress" inventory — just over 22% of the 31,482 total pending cases. This is the largest country-specific backlog on record.

The CBSA is currently processing approximately 400 removals per week nationwide, according to agency spokesperson Kelly Cameron. The federal government allocated $30.4 million under Canada's Border Plan to strengthen the agency's capacity to complete 20,000 removals annually and plans to hire 1,000 new enforcement officers.

What's Driving the Numbers

The surge in Indian deportations reflects several converging factors. A significant share of removals are tied to refused refugee and asylum claims, which have risen sharply as Canada's Immigration and Refugee Board works through its backlog. The majority of ongoing deportation cases — over 27,000 out of 30,733 — involve refugee claimants.

Extortion-related crime has also driven enforcement action. The CBSA opened 484 immigration investigations linked to extortion as of June 18, 2026, issuing 139 removal orders and completing 81 deportations. While the agency has not released nationality-specific breakdowns for the extortion crackdown, all publicly identified deportees — roughly two dozen — have been Indian nationals.

Indian nationals also represent Canada's largest international student population and one of its biggest groups of temporary foreign workers, spanning manufacturing, food production, hospitality, caregiving, and transportation. When a nationality has such a large presence in the temporary resident system, even modest non-compliance rates produce significant absolute numbers.

The Historical Trajectory

The acceleration has been steep. Canada deported just 625 Indian nationals in 2019. By 2025, the number had risen to 3,779. The first-half 2026 figures suggest the full-year total could approach or exceed 6,000 — roughly ten times the 2019 level.

In 2025, Canada removed 23,160 people overall, spending approximately $78 million on the process. The majority were asylum seekers whose claims had been rejected.

What This Means for the Indian Diaspora

The numbers arrive at a sensitive moment in the Canada-India relationship, already strained by the diplomatic crisis over the assassination of Sikh activist Hardeep Singh Nijjar in 2023. Both countries expelled senior diplomats in the fallout.

For the estimated 1.8 million Canadians of Indian descent and the roughly 900,000 Indian temporary residents in the country, the enforcement surge creates anxiety that extends beyond those directly affected. Immigration lawyers note that the complexity of Canada's removal process means many deportees have limited access to legal representation during appeals.

The data also feeds a growing narrative of reverse migration. Across 2026, more NRIs have been returning to India from Canada, citing unaffordable costs of living in cities like Toronto and Vancouver, family priorities, and a changing India with rising salaries and rapid infrastructure growth.
